113408750.title: File:Hoe schadelijk is plastic voor onze gezondheid.webm

ImageDescription.value: #Microplastics, je ademt ze in en eet ze op. En helaas, je kunt er niet aan ontkomen, want ze zitten tegenwoordig overal. Wetenschappers maken zich zorgen om al die plasticdeeltjes in ons lichaam en doen er daarom veel onderzoek naar. Immunoloog Nienke Vrisekoop (UMC Utrecht) praat je bij over de meest recente kennis en onderzoeken over die piepkleine plastics. Om nu eindelijk antwoord te krijgen op die ene vraag: hoe #schadelijk zijn die microplastics nou echt?

160605938.title: File:Impact et devenir des microplastiques dans les écosystèmes marins (Ifremer 00652-76425).webm

ImageDescription.value:
MICRO is a project in which five scientific institutes studied the presence and impact of microplastics in the Interreg 2 Seas region and the English Channel region. It was a cooperation between the Belgian Agricultural and Fisheries Research Institute (ILVO), the Centre for Environmental, Fisheries and Aquaculture Sciences (CEFAS) in the United Kingdom, the Dutch foundation Stichting Deltares and two French partners, Ifremer and CNRS.

The project started on July 1, 2012 and the cross-border partnership was implemented until the end of September 2014.

160666125.title: File:L'Ifremer au sein du projet Preventing Plastic Pollution (Ifremer 00677-78912).webm

ImageDescription.value: Preventing Plastic Pollution works in partnership with 18 organisations from France and England, and seeks to understand and reduce the impacts of plastic pollution on the marine environment. Looking from source to sea, the project will identify and target where plastic accumulates, embed behaviour change within local communities and businesses, and implement effective solutions and alternatives.

160617351.title: File:L'ingestion des micro-plastiques par les animaux marins (Ifremer 00642-75442).webm

ImageDescription.value:
In the ocean, plastic waste generates billions of particles through fragmentation: microplastics. These can be ingested by animals. The physiological impact of this ingestion has, until now, been little studied. Microplastics have been found in the stomach and on the gills of fish, but also inside other marine organisms. Ifremer is seeking to better understand the impact of this ingestion on the feeding, reproduction and growth of marine organisms.

This film was made using computer-generated images.

160593439.title: File:La formation des micro-plastiques par fragmentation (Ifremer 00642-75441).webm

ImageDescription.value:
Man produces about 300 million tons of plastic each year. A significant portion of this waste ends up in the sea, most often via rivers. These plastics are subject to attacks that will, little by little, fragment the objects into thousands of pieces of different sizes. Wind and waves exert mechanical constraints; oxygen in the air, chemical constraints through oxidation; and light, a molecular destructuring through the action of ultraviolet radiation.

Fragmentation is not uniform. Some pieces are quite large: they are called macro-waste. Others are very small, often invisible to the naked eye: they are micro and nano-plastics. Micro-plastics are fragments between 5 mm and 1 µm in size. By comparison, the diameter of a hair is between 40 and 60 µm.

These different particles are found on the surface, in open water or at the bottom of the oceans. But, currently, we lose track of a significant portion of the plastic thrown into the sea. To solve this scientific enigma, Ifremer is developing innovative approaches for detecting the smallest plastic particles.

This film was made using computer-generated images.

160658711.title: File:Les micro-plastiques, vecteurs de contamination chimique et biologique (Ifremer 00644-75637).webm

ImageDescription.value:
In the ocean, plastic waste generates particles through fragmentation: microplastics. Estimated at 5,000 billion, these particles represent an immense cumulative surface area, which microalgae, bacteria and viruses colonize. This new marine ecosystem is called the plastisphere.

Microplastics also act like a magnet, concentrating chemical pollutants found in the sea on their surface: this is called absorption.

Transported by ocean currents, microplastics can travel long distances. They are therefore vectors of biological and chemical contaminants, which can be ingested by marine animals. At Ifremer, researchers are studying the impact of this plastic pollution on marine ecosystems, and in particular on the seafood we consume.

This film was made using computer-generated images.

193242996.title: File:The War on Microplastics with Dr. Leo Trasande.webm

ImageDescription.value:
In this episode, I sit down with Dr. Leo Trasande, one of the country’s leading experts on environmental health and toxic exposures, to discuss the growing threat of microplastics, PFAS, and endocrine-disrupting chemicals.

We explore how these substances are affecting fertility, metabolism, brain development, chronic disease, and long-term public health—and why the economic costs are staggering. Dr. Trasande explains how plastics enter the body, what they may be doing once they’re there, and what Americans can do to reduce exposure.

We also discuss HHS’s new STOMP initiative and the effort to understand and confront the impact of toxic chemicals on human health.

Artist.value: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

149930630.title: File:Zit er echt plastic in al ons eten.webm

ImageDescription.value:
Microplastics zitten overal en dus ook in je lijf. Want je eet ze op, je ademt ze in en je smeert ze zelfs op je huid. Na de Tweede Wereldoorlog zijn we héél veel plastic beginnen gebruiken en daardoor kan je niet meer ontkomen aan de kleine restantjes, de micro- en zelfs nanoplastics. Maar wetenschappers maken zich zorgen om al die plasticdeeltjes in ons lichaam. Dr. Nelly Saenen, toxicoloog aan de UHasselt, doet daarom onderzoek naar hoe die piepkleine plastics juist in ons lichaam terechtkomen en of ze daar veel schade aanrichten.
